DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 24SMCV01804    Hearing Date: March 5, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

MAYA KADOSH,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

MOUSSA MASJEDI, et al.,  

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  24SMCV01804 

  

  Hearing Date: March 5, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  defendant’s motion to conform  

  order to justice 

 

 

 

 

This hearing is on Defendant Moussa Masjedi’s motion to conform order to justice.  According to Defendant, when the Court vacated its dismissal of Plaintiff’s complaint, it did not address Defendant’s pending discovery disputes with Plaintiff Maya Kadosh.  Defendant claims Plaintiff has failed to answer Defendant’s request for production (set one), request for admissions (set one), and form interrogatories (set one).  Defendant asks that the Court “conform” its January 30, 2026 order vacating the dismissal to require Plaintiff to respond to these discovery requests. 

However, Defendant has not filed any motions to compel for the Court to consider.  Moreover, while there was an informal discovery conference scheduled by Defendant for November 5, 2025, Defendant never appeared for the IDC, and accordingly, he did not comply with this Department’s rules requiring an IDC before any discovery motions can be filed.   

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES Defendant’s motion to conform order to justice. 

  

 

IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED: March 5, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 25SMCV06383    Hearing Date: March 5, 2026    Dept: 205

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

LUIS ARTURO VALDIVIA JR.,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

GUARDIAN INTERNATIONAL SOLUTIONS, INC., et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV06383 

  Hearing Date: March 5, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  Defendant’s DEMURRER TO  

  complaint  

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a constructive termination case.  Plaintiff Luis Arturo Valdivia Jr. worked for Defendant Guardian International Solutions, Inc. as a security guard from March 2023 to March 2025.  Plaintiff claims that Defendant would issue paychecks that bounced because of insufficient funds.  Plaintiff also alleges Defendant denied him meal and rest breaks.  Because of these alleged labor code violations, Plaintiff claims he was forced to resign. 

The operative complaint alleges claims for (1) wrongful discharge in violation of public policy, (2) unlawful wage practices, (3) meal and rest period violations, (4) waiting time penalties, and (5) failure to provide records and inspections in a timely manner.  

This hearing is on Defendant’s demurrer to the Complaint.  Defendant argues that all the claims are barred because Plaintiff failed to exhaust his administrative remedies as required under Labor Code section 2699.3 and 2699.5.  Additionally, Defendant argues there was no discharge because Plaintiff has not alleged that the working conditions were so intolerable or aggravated that he was compelled to resign.   

   

MEET AND CONFER 

Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41 requires that before the filing of a demurrer the moving party “shall meet and confer in person or by telephone” with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to demurrer for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer.  (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a).)  The parties are to meet and confer at least five days before the date the responsive pleading is due. (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a)(2).)  Thereafter, the moving party shall file and serve a declaration detailing their meet and confer efforts. (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.41(a)(3).)  Defendants submit the declaration of Tom Yu who attests the parties met and conferred by telephone but could not resolve the issues raised in the demurrer.  This satisfies Defendants’ meet and confer obligations.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“[A] demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the allegations in a complaint.” (Lewis v. Safeway, Inc. (2015) 235 Cal.App.4th 385, 388.)  A demurrer can be used only to challenge defects that appear on the face of the pleading under attack or from matters outside the pleading that are judicially noticeable.  (See Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994 (in ruling on a demurrer, a court may not consider declarations, matters not subject to judicial notice, or documents not accepted for the truth of their contents).)  For purposes of ruling on a demurrer, all facts pleaded in a complaint are assumed to be true, but the reviewing court does not assume the truth of conclusions of law. (Aubry v. Tri-City Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)   

Leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (See Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 349 (court shall not “sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is any reasonable possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment”); Kong v. City of Hawaiian Gardens Redevelopment Agency (2002) 108 Cal.App.4th 1028, 1037 (“A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally construed, can state a cause of action under any theory or if there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured by amendment.”). The burden is on the complainant to show the Court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) 

DISCUSSION 

Defendants argue that Plaintiff’s claims are barred by the exhaustion requirements in Labor Code sections 2699.3 and 2699.5.  The Court disagrees. 

The Labor Code Private Attorney General (“PAG”) Act provides in relevant part at¿section 2699, subdivision (a):¿ “Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any provision of this code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the [LWDA] or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, for a violation of this code,¿may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of himself or herself and other current or former employees pursuant to the procedures specified in¿Section 2699.3.” (Italics added.) 

In 2004, the Act was amended to include a new section, section¿2699.3, requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies prior to commencement of a civil action.  Section 2699.3, subdivision (a)’s administrative procedures apply to actions to recover civil penalties for alleged violations of numerous Labor Code provisions¿specifically identified in¿section 2699.5.  In particular, the¿“provisions of subdivision¿(a) of Section 2699.3 shall apply to any alleged violation of the following provisions: … Section … 201, … 203, … 204, … 212… .” (Labor Code, § 2699.5.) 

The Complaint here seeks statutory penalties, not civil penalties.  In Dunlap v. Superior Court (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 330, the court recognized that there is a difference between statutory penalties and civil penalties, and that the PAG Act’s prefiling notice and exhaustion requirements “are triggered when an aggrieved employee seeks civil penalties for violation of a Labor Code provision that previously provided for recovery of a civil penalty by the Labor Commissioner.” (Id. at 341 (emphasis added).)  

In Dunlap, a former employee sued his employer (a bank) for alleged violations of California's Labor Code.  The trial court struck the former employee’s claims for statutory penalties on the ground he failed to exhaust his administrative remedies in accordance with the PAG Act.  The appellate court issued a writ of mandate directing the lower court to vacate its order striking the complaint.  The Dunlap court held that the PAG Act’s administrative prerequisites to filing suit did not apply because the only penalties sought by the former employee were various statutory penalties, and these penalties were already recoverable by employees prior to the adoption of the PAG Act.  (Id. at 341-343.)  

So it is here.  The Complaint seeks statutory penalties, not civil penalties, and therefore, the pre-filing and exhaustion requirements of the PAG Act do not apply. 

Defendant also argues that Plaintiff’s first cause of action for constructive discharge fails because the delayed payment of wages and denial of rest and meal breaks are insufficient to establish a claim for¿constructive¿discharge.  The Court disagrees. 

“[T]o establish a constructive discharge, an employee must plead¿and prove . . . that the employer either intentionally created or knowingly permitted working conditions that were so intolerable or aggravated at the time of the employee's resignation that a reasonable employer would realize that a reasonable person in the employee’s position would be compelled to resign.” (Vasquez v. Franklin Management Real Estate Fund, Inc.¿(2013) 222 Cal.App.4th 819, 826.) 

The court in¿Vasquez v. Franklin Management Real Estate Fund, Inc., supra, 222 Cal.App.4th 819¿looked at whether wage claims like a¿failure¿to¿pay¿minimum wages or a¿failure¿to reimburse business expenses could support a¿constructive¿discharge¿claim.¿The court concluded that under the facts presented, “California's minimum wage law represents a fundamental policy for purposes of a claim for wrongful termination or constructive discharge in violation of public policy.” (Id.¿at 831-832.) The court held allegations that the defendant's employer failed to reimburse its employee for business expenses including mileage, which resulted in the employee effectively being paid less than minimum wage, were sufficient to support a claim for constructive discharge.  (Id.¿at 828.) 

The facts in Vasquez are analogous to those here.  Plaintiff claims Defendant repeatedly delayed in paying his wages and denied him rest and meal breaks.  A reasonable jury could conclude that these labor code violations created an intolerable condition, forcing Plaintiff to resign.  

Defendant argues that the conditions were not intolerable because Plaintiff continued working for Defendant for five months after the alleged late wage payments.  Defendant cites no authority for the proposition that an employee must resign immediately after an intolerable condition occurs in order to claim a constructive discharge.  Defendant’s argument may be relevant on summary judgment or at trial, but it does not preclude a claim for constructive discharge at the pleading stage.     

 Defendant also argues that Plaintiff cannot state a constructive discharge claim because “if the employee quits without giving the employer a reasonable chance to resolve the problem, the employee is not constructively discharged.”  As support, Defendant cites to an Eighth Circuit opinion applying Minnesota law.  (See Bergslrom-Ek v. Best Oil Co. (8th Cir. 1998) 153 F.3d 851.)  Notwithstanding, Defendant’s argument finds support in California law.   

In Turner v. Anheuser-Busch (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1238, held that “[b] y requiring employees to notify someone in a position of authority of their plight, we permit employers unaware of any wrongdoing to correct a potentially destructive situation, and we prevent employers from shielding themselves from constructive discharge lawsuits simply by deliberately ignoring a situation that has become intolerable to a reasonable employee.”  (Id. at 1250.)  

Under Turner, therefore, Plaintiff is required to allege that he notified Defendant of the alleged labor code violations so that Defendant has an opportunity to correct it.  There is no such allegation in the Complaint, and accordingly, the Court sustains the demurrer with 20 days’ leave to amend. 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court OVERRULES IN PART and SUSTAINS IN PART the demurrer to the Complaint with 20 days’ leave to amend.
